newsitem.title: USA: Bigger British Europe role to aid U.S. ties -Cook.
newsitem.headline: Bigger British Europe role to aid U.S. ties -Cook.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said on Monday the new Labour government's commitment to playing a leading role in Europe should be seen as an opportunity, not a hindrance, for U.S.-British ties.

Cook said senior officials he met in Washingon on Monday, including Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, expressed understanding of that position and "wished us well in our drive to achieve a better, stronger relationship with Europe".

"A Britain that is a leading player in Europe will be a more useful and a more valued ally of the United States than a Britain, which, under the previous government, was drifting into a marginalized offshore island," he told a news conference.

It was the first meeting between Albright and Cook since the overwhelming May 1 victory of the Labour Party, which has promised to play a more prominent role in an increasingly integrated European Union.
Cook, on a one-day visit which also included meetings with Defence Secretary William Cohen and senior congressmen, said his talks here were harmonious.
But he introduced a jarring note by raising serious doubts over a July 1998 deadline for pulling the international peacekeeping force out of Bosnia, a date that Washington sees as fixed.
Cook said the 1995 Dayton peace accords for Bosnia could not be judged a success without fulfilling one of their key provisions -- the integration of the Bosnia, Serb and Croat ethnic nationalities.

"At the present time we have to be quite frank and recognise that we have not made the progress towards that (that) we would wish," he said. As examples, he noted the factions had not even agreed on a coordinated car number plate system and had no integrated telephone system.
"We have agreed that we must redouble our efforts" to achieve the integration envisaged in Dayton, he said.
"Without that, I must say quite frankly, it may be difficult for us to contemplate a military withdrawal by the middle of next year," he added.
At the same time, he said that if the United States pulled its forces out, Britain and its European partners would definitely withdraw as well. "One out, all out," he said.
He said those involved in the peace process would review the situation around the turn of the year to establish whether the conditions allowed a withdrawal.

The United States and Britain put out a joint statement saying they would support an international conference in London before the end of this year to thrash out the issue of Nazi gold transfers during World War Two.

Cook said the aim of the conference would be to establish the facts about the gold amassed by the Nazis from conquests and by confiscation from individuals and to consider possible restitution for individuals and Nazi groups.
The United States issued a report earlier this month blaming Switzerland for buying Nazi gold and for its stonewalling attitude over the issue in the post-war years.
